title: Dedicated Capacity QoS, Burst Fallback, and Isolation Controls PRD
creator: Ariana Patel
overview: This PRD defines requirements for a unified QoS and fallback framework for Redwood Dedicated capacity. The goal is to give customers predictable latency and throughput guarantees while enabling controlled, auditable bursting and safe isolation between tenants and workloads.
background: Customers using Dedicated pools have requested clearer QoS controls: the ability to reserve baseline capacity, allow controlled short-term bursts, and guarantee isolation for compliance-sensitive workloads. Existing implementations are fragmented (reserved pools + ad-hoc autoscale rules + manual runbooks). This effort consolidates policy, runtime enforcement, and console UX into a coherent feature set.
problem_statement: Without a consistent QoS framework customers experience unpredictable latency under contention, unclear billing for transient bursts, and difficulty demonstrating isolation for compliance. Engineering teams spend time tuning per-customer policies and responding to incidents caused by noisy neighbors or misconfigured burst rules.
goals: 1) Deliver a declarative QoS policy model for Dedicated pools (baseline reservation, headroom, burst tokens, cooldowns). 2) Implement deterministic runtime enforcement and metering so customers can rely on latency and throughput SLOs. 3) Provide console APIs and SDK hooks to configure policies and view audit logs and cost impact. 4) Default safe fallback behaviors when capacity is constrained (model variant fallback, route to shared pool, graceful degradation).
non_goals: 1) Re-architecting the serving runtime internals unrelated to enforcement (micro-optimizations out of scope). 2) Implementing new billing models — cost reporting will use existing usage metrics. 3) Multi-region orchestration for Dedicated pools (initial rollout limited to single-region Dedicated deployments).
user_stories: As a platform admin I want to create a dedicated pool with a 10qps baseline and 50qps burst for 5 minutes so my product team’s peak traffic is absorbed without manual intervention.
As a compliance lead I want to pin a pool to 'isolation=true' so traffic from regulated clients never shares GPU hosts with other tenants.
As an SRE I want automatic fallback to a smaller model variant and a runbook-triggered notification when burst capacity is exhausted so customer-facing latency remains bounded.
As an engineering manager I want visibility into burst usage and cost impact per customer so we can evaluate capacity commits vs usage.
requirements: Policy model: support 'baseline', 'headroom', 'burst_window_seconds', 'burst_capacity_units', 'cooldown_seconds', and 'isolation_level' fields in pool config.
Enforcement: runtime must enforce reservation semantics such that baseline capacity is always available to pinned tenants; headroom and burst are rate-limited and preemptible.
Burst accounting: track burst consumption in real-time and persist per-customer burst events to the audit log for 90 days.
Fallback policies: support declarative fallbacks: (a) model_variant_fallback, (b) route_to_shared_pool, (c) queue-with-timeout + structured error response.
Isolation controls: 'isolation_level' options: 'soft' (shared hosts but scheduling preference), 'hard' (strict host-level tenancy), 'network-only' (network namespace isolation).
Console & API: console UI and REST/SDK endpoints for creating/updating QoS policies, a cost-impact simulator, and per-pool activity timeline visualization.
SLOs: for baseline traffic p95 latency delta <= 20% vs. dedicated lab baseline; for burst traffic, documented best-effort latency and clear indicators in console.
Auditing & RBAC: policy changes must be recorded with user, timestamp, and diff; only users with 'pool-admin' role can change isolation_level and baseline reservations.
Testing: automated load tests that validate policy enforcement across 3 host topologies and chaos tests that simulate host loss and forced demotion of burst capacity.
Backward compatibility: existing reserved pools without explicit policies should default to baseline=previous_commit and burst disabled.
edge_cases: Simultaneous bursts from multiple customers exhausting pooled headroom — system should enforce fair-share degradation and emit actionable alerts.
A pool with hard isolation depleting reserved GPUs due to long-running inference: should queue new requests with configured max_queue_ms and return structured error after timeout.
Policy updates mid-burst — changes to burst parameters should be applied atomically on the next allocation window; current in-flight bursts complete under the prior policy.
Interplay with autoscaling: autoscale triggers must respect 'min_reservation' and not scale down below baseline; scaling down should respect cooldowns to avoid flip-flopping.
acceptance_criteria: Create/update pool API: create a Dedicated pool with baseline, headroom, and burst fields — API returns 200 and pool state reflects provided fields.

Enforcement correctness: under controlled load test (50% baseline + 150% burst across 10 tenants), baseline requests for pinned tenants observe p95 latency within 20% of lab baseline while burst requests are rate-limited according to burst_capacity_units.
Burst accounting & logs: burst consumption events appear in audit logs and console timeline; sample retention spot-check shows data persisted for 90 days in the test cluster.

Fallback behavior: when burst exhausted, requests are routed to configured fallback (e.g., model_variant_fallback) and responses include standard structured error or downgraded output; integration test covers all fallback modes.
Isolation enforcement: single-tenant 'hard' isolation pools never co-locate other tenant workloads on hosts in 100% of randomized placement tests across three runs.
RBAC and audit: attempts to change isolation_level by non-pool-admin user are blocked with 403 and an audit record is created.
Console UX: cost simulator shows estimated cost delta for a sample policy change within +/- 15% of measured synthetic-job cost in staging.
Resilience: during host failure scenario the system preserves baseline reservations for surviving hosts within feasible capacity and emits a post-incident summary with impacted customers identified.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (private beta): enable on 3 pilot customers in a single region; disable cross-customer bursting and require explicit opt-in. Monitor SLOs and billing signals for 4 weeks.
Phase 2 (broader beta): open to customers with Dedicated contracts; enable controlled cross-customer headroom with conservative global caps and enable console cost simulator.
Phase 3 (GA): graduate policies to GA with default safe limits, documentation, and upgrade guides. Enable multi-region awareness in a follow-up iteration.
Safety gates: rollback criteria include >5% of baseline requests experiencing p95 regression >40% across pilot customers or detection of billing anomalies >10% vs forecast for pilot pools.
monitoring_and_metrics: Per-pool metrics: baseline_utilization, headroom_utilization, burst_consumed_units, burst_events_per_minute.
Latency metrics: p50/p95/p99 for baseline vs burst vs fallback paths, tracked per model variant.
SLO dashboards: percent of baseline requests meeting latency SLO, burst_fallback_rate, queue_drop_rate.
Alerts: sustained baseline SLO breaches for >5 minutes, sudden spike in burst_consumption >x% of configured cap, or policy enforcement errors.
dependencies: Runtime: kernel-level token bucket scheduler and eviction hooks (ENG-Related work planned in runtime Q4).
Console: policy editor UI, cost simulator, and timeline visualization (Console-UX team).
Billing: maps burst units to cost buckets and surfacing in invoices (Billing team).
Auth/RBAC: support for 'pool-admin' role and audit logging plumbing (Security/SSO team).
E2E testing infra: synthetic workload generators and chaos engineering harness (SRE).
open_questions: What unit should 'burst_capacity_units' use? tokens, qps-equivalent, or a normalized cost unit? Proposal: start with qps-equivalent for rate-based models and normalize for token-based models in next iteration.
Should default pools have any ephemeral burst allowance? Current proposal: default to burst disabled to protect existing customers from surprise billing.
How aggressive should autoscale be when headroom is routinely exhausted? Option A: proactive scale to target concurrency; Option B: prefer immediate fallback and human review.
decision_log: 2025-11-14: Agreed to represent burst as time-windowed 'burst_capacity_units' and document mapping guidance for token vs qps models (decision by Platform and Product).
2025-11-17: Scoped initial GA to single-region Dedicated pools and postponed multi-region orchestration to follow-up release.
testing_plan: Unit tests for policy parsing and merge semantics.
Integration tests exercising the three fallback modes (variant, shared-pool, queue-with-timeout) with simulated throttling.
Load tests: run 4-hour surge tests to validate burst accounting and headroom exhaustion behavior across 10 tenants.
Chaos tests: simulate GPU host termination and validate baseline preservation behavior and incident notifications.
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Misconfigured burst policies cause unexpected billing impact. Mitigation: console cost simulator + opt-in for cross-customer bursting + guardrails on default burst caps.
Risk: Hard isolation increases packing inefficiency and cost. Mitigation: document trade-offs and provide recommended capacity-sizing tooling and cost estimates in console.
Risk: Autoscale flip-flop near threshold. Mitigation: add cooldown windows and require min_reservation honoring before scale-down.
notes: Scope change log: originally planned symmetric cross-customer bursting in Phase 1; changed to opt-in per pool after customer feedback. Also deferred multi-region placement to reduce surface area for initial rollout.
